title: Neil deGrasse Tyson Explains Why Time Travel to the Future Is Possible
excerpt: Astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson explains how traveling at high speeds could allow humans to reach the future while ruling out travel to the past.

Traveling into the future may be possible under the laws of physics, but returning to the past is a different matter, astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson explained during an appearance on Hot Ones Game Night. On the October 14 episode, host Joe Santagato asked Tyson whether humans could ever travel through time, prompting an explanation of how motion through space can affect the passage of time.

Tyson described a scenario in which a person travels at high speed through space and experiences less elapsed time than people who remain on Earth. Depending on the traveler's speed, the difference could mean that minutes pass for the traveler while hours, days, or years pass for those on the planet.

According to Tyson, this effect would allow someone to arrive in Earth's future without possessing the ability to return to an earlier point in time. His explanation distinguished the physical possibility of moving forward through time from the fictional concept of traveling backward into history.

When Santagato initially asked whether humans would ever be able to time travel, Tyson first gave a brief negative response before clarifying the distinction between traveling to the future and traveling to the past.

"We can time travel to the future, but not the past." Tyson explained.

The astrophysicist expanded on the concept by describing how differences in speed could produce different amounts of elapsed time for a space traveler and people who stayed on Earth.

"If I accelerate you through space for a while, and you age, let's say 10 minutes, and I bring you back to Earth, depending on what speed I sent you, we could have aged an hour, a day, a year. You went into the future. Not into your own future.

You went into everybody else's future." Tyson said.

He further characterized the phenomenon as a form of time travel while emphasizing the limits of an individual's movement through their own timeline.

"It's a form of time travel, but there's no way for you to go into your own future. No. You are a prisoner of the present in your timeline, forever transitioning between your inaccessible past and your unknowable future." Tyson said.

Tyson's explanation did not endorse the time-travel scenarios depicted in science fiction films, including Marvel's Avengers movies. His comments focused on the possibility of reaching a future shaped by differences in elapsed time rather than traveling freely between historical periods.

The October 14 appearance also featured a discussion about the relative intelligence of several prominent science figures. Santagato asked Tyson to rank Bill Nye, Stephen Hawking, Carl Sagan, and Tyson himself from most to least intelligent.

Tyson placed Hawking at the top of his ranking, describing him as the leading figure among the group after Albert Einstein. He then discussed Sagan's intellectual abilities before addressing the comparison between himself and Nye.

"Definitely Stephen Hawking, top shelf right there, okay? The undisputed champion. Well, post-Einstein, yes.

And I'd say next, Carl Sagan was a smart guy. Yeah, I'll put him ahead of me there." Tyson said.

For the remaining positions, Tyson said he and Nye were friends and appeared similar in intellectual ability. Rather than placing one above the other, he ranked them jointly in third place.

The appearance combined Tyson's explanation of time and motion with a discussion of well-known science communicators and theoretical physicists. The program's time-travel exchange centered on the distinction between moving into Earth's future through differences in elapsed time and attempting to revisit the past.
